claims.text: A minor addition of an element with strong chemical affinity for phosphorus will improve the glass-forming ability of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy.
The same addition will increase the thermal stability of the alloy's amorphous state.
The additive can be selected according to its propensity to form a stable local bonding environment with phosphorus.
The added element will bond locally with phosphorus in the amorphous structure.
Additive–phosphorus bonding will disrupt preferred crystalline nucleation sites.
Strong local additive–phosphorus bonds will stabilize the disordered amorphous network.
This local bonding will hinder the atomic rearrangements required for crystallization.
Hindering crystallization-related atomic rearrangements will enhance glass-forming ability and amorphous-state thermal stability.
The intervention is expected to work under conventional rapid-solidification conditions.
The intervention should work only over a phosphorus-content range that permits local bonding modification without unwanted phase separation.
Excessive additive concentration may eliminate the beneficial effect.
A base composition that strongly favors crystalline-phase formation may prevent the intervention from being effective.
Formation of additive-containing intermetallic compounds or phase separation may prevent improvement in glass stability.
Relative to an additive-free control, the modified alloy should have a higher crystallization-onset temperature.
Relative to an additive-free control, the modified alloy should have an increased critical cooling rate necessary for crystallization.
Relative to an additive-free control, the modified alloy should exhibit a wider temperature interval between glass transition and crystallization.

contradictions.description: Improved glass-forming ability conventionally corresponds to a lower critical cooling rate required to avoid crystallization, whereas the predicted outcome and falsification rule require an increased critical cooling rate. The rate's definition is not clarified, making its stated direction inconsistent with the principal outcome.
